sections.body: Energy can't be created or destroyed. It changes form: chemical → kinetic (movement) → thermal (heat), and so on.
A CIRCUIT needs a complete loop, an energy source (cell/battery) and components (bulbs, motors).
SERIES circuit: one loop. If one bulb breaks, all go out. PARALLEL circuit: several branches. Others stay on if one breaks.
Most homes are wired in parallel, so turning off one light doesn't turn off the others.

quiz.q: Two bulbs are in series and one blows. What happens to the other?
hints: In series there's only one path.
Old-style fairy lights in series all went dark when one bulb failed.
quiz.explain: In a series circuit the loop is broken, so the other bulb goes out.

quiz.q: A battery-powered fan converts energy mainly from…
hints: Where is the energy stored in a battery?
What does a fan do: move or glow?
A torch converts chemical energy to light energy. A fan produces movement instead.
quiz.explain: The battery's chemical energy becomes kinetic (movement) energy.

quiz.q: A light bulb in a circuit feels warm. What does this show about energy?
options: Some energy is changed into heat (thermal energy), not destroyed
The bulb is creating extra energy
The energy disappears once it leaves the battery
hints: The lesson's first rule: energy can't be created or destroyed. So what CAN it do?
If energy can't vanish, where is some of it going when the bulb feels warm?
When you rub your hands together, kinetic (movement) energy turns into thermal energy, and your hands warm up.
quiz.explain: Energy can't be created or destroyed; it changes form. A bulb changes the energy from the battery into light, and some into thermal energy (heat), which is why it feels warm.
